safetyNote: Avoid eating Coprinopsis atramentaria. It contains coprine and can cause an acetaldehyde (disulfiram-like) reaction if alcohol is consumed with it or during the following 72 hours. Rapid flushing, headache, dizziness, sweating, vomiting, palpitations and low blood pressure can occur; seek poison-centre advice if exposure or symptoms are suspected. The German mycological society places it on its toxic mushroom list.

sections.title: Identification
sections.text: The common inkcap has a 3–7 cm, sometimes larger, grey to grey-brown cap, egg-shaped when young and later broadly bell-shaped. Its mostly smooth surface shows fine lengthwise grooves, especially toward the edge, with a few tiny flattened scales near the crown. The cap does not have the conspicuous white shaggy locks of Coprinus comatus. White to pale grey, slender stems may be hollow in maturity; an obvious persistent ring is absent, though faint veil remains may occur.

sections.title: Gills and ink
sections.text: Crowded gills are free or narrowly attached, at first pale grey-white, then brown-grey to black. The cap margin tears, turns upward and digests itself into black liquid as the gills mature. The spore deposit is black. A single colour in a static drawing cannot convey this sequence, so inspect specimens at different stages.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: Saprobic on dead wood, often from buried hardwood, stumps or woody debris. It commonly fruits in dense clusters that seem to emerge from lawns, gardens, pathsides and parks because the wood is below the soil. In Europe it is seen mainly from spring through autumn, sometimes into early winter.

sections.title: Coprine and lookalikes
sections.text: Coprine interferes with alcohol metabolism, leading to a rapid acetaldehyde-type reaction when alcohol is taken during or up to 72 hours after the mushroom meal. Symptoms can include facial and neck flushing, headache, dizziness, nausea or vomiting, sweating and low blood pressure. Coprinellus micaceus tends to be smaller and warmer brown with mica-like veil granules on young caps; Coprinus comatus is taller, white and shaggy. These distinctions are for recognition, not a decision to eat.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The white-background plate presents a cluster of whole grey, finely grooved fruit bodies, one older cap beginning to liquefy at its black margin, a longitudinal cut revealing gills and a hollowing stem, and the darkening crowded gills viewed from below.
